title: Python Agent Engineering
description: Master local-first Python agent engineering from virtual environments and typed tools to persistent memory, grounded retrieval, evaluation harnesses, and human-in-the-loop control.

target.learner: A beginner who can use a Windows computer but is not expected to know Python, APIs, databases, language models, or agent frameworks.
target.professionalOutcome: Design, build, evaluate, secure, and operate a local-first Python personal agent with replaceable providers, bounded tools, durable state, grounded answers, and human control.
specialGoals: Use Python rather than JavaScript for every learner coding outcome.
Remain completable with free software, a deterministic FakeModel, and local fixtures; paid model access is optional.
Prefer transparent Python implementations before framework abstractions.
Graduate with three cumulative portfolio projects and inspectable evidence of production readiness.

phases.title: Python Foundations
phases.outcome: Write, debug, test, and persist small Python command-line programs using isolated environments, typed structures, and structured files.

phases.title: Reliable Python Systems
phases.outcome: Build resilient Python services with automated pytest suites, test doubles, robust HTTP client boundaries, and typed CLI interfaces managed in Git.

phases.title: LLM Application Foundations
phases.outcome: Interface with LLM gateways via structural protocols, enforce typed prompt and output contracts, validate tool schemas, and manage bounded conversation contexts.

phases.title: Agent Engineering Core
phases.outcome: Build autonomous ReAct control loops with safe action boundaries, SQLite durable storage, and grounded local retrieval with verifiable citations.

phases.title: Reliability, Observability, and Advanced Control
phases.outcome: Harden agent systems with automated evaluation benchmark suites, structured step-level tracing, asyncio background workflows, security permission matrices, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) integrations.

phases.title: Production Personal Agent
phases.outcome: Architect, package, evaluate, and operate an end-to-end local personal agent with modular specialist routing, pyproject.toml distribution, and continuous verification.

prompts.prompt: How does activating a virtual environment alter PowerShell environment variables like PATH, and why is this critical for reproducible projects?
When might an unactivated script accidentally run using a global Python interpreter, and how does your CLI diagnose this condition?

skillCheck.title: Python Workspace and First CLI Skill Check
skillCheck.instructions: Answer all 10 questions. A score of 7/10 (70%) passes. Review the explanations before any recovery attempt.

questions.prompt: A developer installs third-party packages globally with pip and inadvertently breaks dependencies for another project. What standard Python practice prevents this problem?

options.label: Rename the global Python executable for each project
Install all packages as Administrator to override conflicts
Create and activate a project-local virtual environment using python -m venv
Store all project files in a single root directory

questions.explanation: Virtual environments provide isolated directory trees containing their own Python interpreter and site-packages folder, preventing package version conflicts between different projects.

questions.prompt: PowerShell blocks .\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1. Which command changes the policy only for the current PowerShell process, so closing that shell removes the change?

options.label: Set-ExecutionPolicy -ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -Scope Process
Set-ExecutionPolicy -ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -Scope CurrentUser
Set-ExecutionPolicy -ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -Scope LocalMachine
Set-ExecutionPolicy -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -Scope LocalMachine

questions.explanation: Process scope exists only for the current PowerShell session. CurrentUser and LocalMachine persist beyond that shell, while a machine-wide Bypass setting is unnecessarily broad. First inspect the effective policy and use this troubleshooting step only when activation is actually blocked.

questions.prompt: In a running Python script, what expression reliably evaluates to True when executed inside an active virtual environment rather than the base installation?

options.label: sys.executable.endswith("python3")
os.name == "nt"
platform.system() == "Windows"
sys.prefix != sys.base_prefix

questions.explanation: In Python 3 virtual environments, sys.prefix points to the virtual environment folder while sys.base_prefix points to the underlying base Python interpreter installation.

questions.prompt: A script executes print("Version: " + sys.version_info.major). What is the result in Python 3?

options.label: It prints "Version: 3" after automatic conversion
It raises a TypeError because strings cannot be concatenated directly with integers using +
It prints "Version: None"
It converts the integer into its ASCII character representation

questions.explanation: Python is strongly typed and does not implicitly coerce integers into strings during concatenation; str(sys.version_info.major) or an f-string is required.

questions.prompt: Which code snippet demonstrates the most idiomatic and readable Python string formatting for reporting variable values?

options.label: "Version: " + str(version) + " Path: " + str(path)
"Version: %s Path: %s" % (version, path)
f"Version: {version} Path: {path}"
"Version: {} Path: {}".format(version, path)

questions.explanation: Formatted string literals (f-strings) introduced in Python 3.6 are concise, readable, and evaluated at runtime with direct variable scope interpolation.

questions.prompt: Why is it standard engineering practice to add the virtual environment directory (e.g. .venv/) to .gitignore?

options.label: Virtual environments contain machine-specific absolute symlinks and binaries that do not work across machines
Git does not permit committing directories with names starting with a period
Committing .venv corrupts the local Python interpreter binaries
The Python Package Index blocks accounts that push virtual environments

questions.explanation: Virtual environments are ephemeral and tied to specific OS paths and architectures; dependencies should be declared in configuration files so environments can be recreated anywhere.

questions.prompt: doctor.py defines EXPECTED_PYTHON_MAJOR = 3 as fixed configuration. The program also reads a user-supplied label. Which design keeps fixed configuration separate from changing input?

options.label: Replace EXPECTED_PYTHON_MAJOR with the text returned by input()
Store both values in the same variable because Python infers their purpose
Declare both names global inside every function that uses them
Leave EXPECTED_PYTHON_MAJOR unchanged and store the input in a separate descriptive variable such as report_label

questions.explanation: A fixed expected value and changing user input have different meanings and lifetimes. Separate descriptive names preserve that distinction and avoid surprising reassignment; uppercase naming is a convention, not runtime enforcement.

questions.prompt: A function calculates whether the active Python major version is supported. Why should it return True or False and let main() print the message?

options.label: Returning a value automatically activates the virtual environment
The returned result can be tested, reused, or formatted differently without coupling the calculation to terminal output
Python functions are not permitted to call print()
A Boolean return value is always faster than an f-string

questions.explanation: Returning the result separates the check from presentation. Calling code can test the Boolean, combine it with other checks, or choose human-readable or JSON output without changing the calculation.

questions.prompt: Which command guarantees that you invoke pip using the Python interpreter of the currently active virtual environment rather than a different global interpreter?

options.label: pip.exe install -U package
where pip install package
python -m pip install package
py -3 pip install package

questions.explanation: Executing python -m pip ensures that pip runs under the exact Python interpreter currently selected by the shell environment, avoiding PATH ambiguity.

questions.prompt: What data type does the built-in function input("Prompt: ") return when a user types the digits 42?

options.label: str
int
float
bytes

questions.explanation: The input() function always reads and returns user input as a string (str), regardless of whether the content consists exclusively of numeric digits.

tasks[task_id]
tasks.find(task_id)
tasks.search(task_id)

questions.prompt: You have a list of task records: tasks = [{"id": 1, "done": False}, {"id": 2, "done": True}, {"id": 3, "done": False}]. Which list comprehension produces a list containing only the incomplete task IDs?

options.label: [t["id"] for t in tasks if t["done"]]
[t["id"] for t in tasks if not t["done"]]
[t["id"] for t in tasks while not t["done"]]
[t for t in tasks if not t["done"]["id"]]

questions.explanation: The condition "if not t['done']" filters records where done is False, and the expression "t['id']" extracts the ID of each matching task.

questions.prompt: A CLI program needs to collect unique categories across hundreds of tasks while discarding duplicates. Which data structure does this automatically?

options.label: list
tuple
set
namedtuple

questions.prompt: While iterating over a dictionary with for key in my_dict:, code inside the loop executes del my_dict[key]. What is the immediate consequence?

options.label: The loop completes normally with keys skipped
The dictionary is converted into an immutable tuple
Python resets the loop counter to zero
Python raises a RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration

questions.explanation: Modifying the size of a dictionary (adding or deleting keys) while directly iterating over it raises a RuntimeError. Instead, iterate over a copy of keys like list(my_dict.keys()).

questions.prompt: What boolean value does Python assign to an empty collection such as [] or {} when evaluated in an if statement?

options.label: True, because the collection exists in memory
None
False, because empty sequences and collections are falsy in Python
It raises an EmptyCollectionError

questions.explanation: In Python, empty sequences and collections (such as "", [], (), {}, set()) have a falsy boolean truth value, evaluating to False in conditions.

questions.prompt: You want a loop to prompt the user repeatedly until they type "quit" or "exit". Which structure models this control flow best?

options.label: A recursive function that calls itself for each user input
A while True: loop that reads input and breaks when the user input matches the exit command
A for loop over range(1000000) that ignores the quit command
A try/finally block without any loop

questions.explanation: A while True loop with an explicit break condition cleanly expresses repeated interaction until a designated exit state is reached, avoiding call stack buildup from recursion.

questions.prompt: What is the key functional difference between a Python list and a Python tuple?

options.label: Lists are immutable; tuples are mutable
Lists can hold strings; tuples can only hold integers
Lists can be indexed; tuples cannot be indexed
Lists are mutable (can be appended or modified); tuples are immutable (cannot be changed after creation)

questions.explanation: Lists can be modified in-place after creation (mutable), whereas tuples cannot be altered once instantiated (immutable), making tuples suitable for fixed records and dictionary keys.

questions.prompt: How do you check whether a specific key "urgent" exists in dictionary task_data?

task_data.has_key("urgent")
task_data.contains("urgent")
"urgent" == task_data.keys

Every module imports both other modules inside its top-level code
Each module uses from other_module import * so Python can resolve the cycle automatically

Runtime rejection of every value that conflicts with an annotation

questions.prompt: Which Python standard library module provides an object-oriented, cross-platform interface for filesystem path manipulation?

options.label: sys
pathlib
fileio
winpath

questions.explanation: pathlib (specifically pathlib.Path) is the standard modern Python module for constructing, resolving, and manipulating filesystem paths cleanly across platforms.

questions.prompt: Why is using the with open(...) as f: context manager preferred over manually calling f.close()?

options.label: It compresses the file automatically
It guarantees that the file handle is properly closed even if an exception occurs during reading or writing
It makes file operations run in the background
Manual close() is deprecated in Python 3

questions.explanation: Context managers execute exit cleanup deterministically; even if an unhandled exception or return occurs within the block, the file descriptor is released immediately.

questions.prompt: Why should an application explicitly use encoding="utf-8" when it owns a portable JSON or text file?

options.label: It makes the file’s text-encoding contract independent of operating-system locale and changing interpreter defaults
UTF-8 causes Path.open() to close the file automatically
Windows security descriptors require UTF-8 for every user file
Python cannot open a text file unless an encoding argument is supplied

questions.explanation: An explicit UTF-8 encoding makes the stored-data contract predictable across machines and Python modes. The default may depend on locale or UTF-8-mode settings, so the curriculum does not claim that every current Windows installation always defaults to cp1252.

questions.prompt: Which save sequence best protects the last complete state from a process interruption while new JSON is being written?

options.label: Open state.json in write mode first, then serialize each task directly into it
Write and close complete valid JSON in a sibling temporary file, then replace state.json with that file
Delete state.json, create an empty replacement, and append one task at a time
Keep state only in a Python variable and write it when the operating system shuts down

questions.explanation: Opening the only good target with "w" truncates it before serialization finishes. Completing and closing a sibling temporary file before replacement prevents readers from seeing a half-written target during an ordinary process interruption. Strong power-loss durability may additionally require platform-specific flush/fsync handling, so replacement is not presented as an absolute hardware guarantee.

questions.prompt: How do json.dump and json.dumps differ in the Python json module?

options.label: json.dump serializes to a file-like stream; json.dumps serializes to a string
json.dump is for dictionaries; json.dumps is for lists
json.dump encrypts data; json.dumps does not
json.dumps is deprecated in favor of json.dump

questions.explanation: json.dump(obj, file_obj) writes JSON directly into an open file pointer, whereas json.dumps(obj) returns the serialized JSON as a Python str.

questions.prompt: When json.loads() encounters malformed JSON in a state file, what exception does it raise?

options.label: ValueError only
SyntaxError
FileCorruptError
json.JSONDecodeError (which inherits from ValueError)

questions.explanation: The json module raises json.JSONDecodeError when parsing fails, providing lineno, colno, and msg attributes explaining where the syntax error occurred.

questions.prompt: Which method on a pathlib.Path object creates parent directories if they do not exist without raising an error if the directory already exists?

options.label: path.make_dir(force=True)
path.create_all()
path.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
os.makedirs(path.str)

questions.explanation: path.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) ensures all missing parent directories are created and quietly succeeds if the target directory already exists.

questions.prompt: Why should persistent application state include a schema_version attribute?

options.label: It is required by the JSON RFC standard
It makes the file read-only on disk
It speeds up json.loads() parsing
It allows future versions of the code to detect older file formats, run migrations, or reject incompatible structures cleanly

questions.explanation: Explicit schema versioning provides software with a reliable contract to inspect stored data shapes, apply migration transformations, or notify users of version changes.

questions.prompt: You have p = Path("data") / "tasks.json". What does p.resolve() do?

options.label: It parses the JSON contents of the file
It converts the path to an absolute, normalized path resolving any symlinks
It creates the file if it is missing
It deletes any sibling files

questions.explanation: Path.resolve() resolves all relative path components, symbolic links, and ".." elements, producing an absolute, normalized path.

questions.prompt: A task dataclass contains a set of tags: tags = {"work", "urgent"}. Why does json.dump(task.__dict__, f) raise a TypeError?

options.label: Sets are mutable
Dataclass fields cannot be serialized to JSON
JSON specifications do not have a set data type; Python sets must be converted to lists before serialization
JSON only supports single-character strings

questions.explanation: JSON supports objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, and null. Python sets are not natively serializable to JSON and must be explicitly converted to lists.

questions.prompt: Why is using a bare except: block (without specifying an exception type) considered a severe anti-pattern in Python?

It catches BaseException, intercepting KeyboardInterrupt, SystemExit, and generator cancellations, making scripts impossible to stop cleanly

questions.prompt: A repository catches an OSError when opening a database and raises DatabaseConnectionError. How should the exception be raised to preserve the original traceback?

raise DatabaseConnectionError(err.traceback)
raise DatabaseConnectionError() with err
raise DatabaseConnectionError() and err

questions.prompt: Which logging level in Python standard logging is intended for reporting regular diagnostic background events during normal application operation?

options.label: CRITICAL
WARNING
INFO
ERROR

questions.prompt: In a try/except/else/finally statement, when does the code inside the else block execute?

options.label: Only when an exception was caught by the except block
Only when no exceptions were raised in the try block
Always, right before the finally block
Only if the finally block fails

questions.explanation: The else block runs only if the try block succeeds without raising any exceptions, keeping success-path code separated from error-handling logic.

questions.prompt: When logging an error inside an except Exception as e: handler, which logger call automatically captures and formats the complete traceback?

options.label: logger.exception("Operation failed")
logger.error("Operation failed: " + str(e))
logger.critical(e)
logger.info("Traceback: %s", sys.exc_info)

questions.explanation: logger.exception() logs a message with level ERROR and automatically attaches the current exception traceback information from sys.exc_info().

questions.prompt: What base class should custom domain exceptions inherit from in standard application code?

options.label: BaseException
StandardError
RuntimeError
Exception

questions.explanation: All non-system-exiting application exceptions should inherit from Exception. Inheriting from BaseException bypasses standard except Exception handlers.

questions.prompt: A web request handler logs: logger.info(f"User request: {request_url} Headers: {headers}"). If headers contains Authorization: Bearer sk-12345, what critical defect exists?

options.label: String formatting inside logging calls is illegal
The logger requires headers to be encoded in binary
Sensitive authentication credentials (API secrets) are written in plain text to log files, creating a durable security vulnerability
INFO level cannot print dictionary contents

questions.explanation: Logging raw authorization headers or secret keys leaks credentials into persistent log files, log management systems, and monitoring dashboards.

questions.prompt: Code contains: try: num = int(text) except ValueError: num = 0. What principle does this demonstrate?

options.label: Broad exception catching
Narrow exception handling targeting only the specific expected failure mode
Silent crash suppression
Type coercion circumvention

questions.explanation: Narrow exception handling catches only the specific error anticipated (ValueError from int conversion), allowing unrelated bugs (like typos or memory errors) to surface.

questions.prompt: Why should library and service modules use logging.getLogger(__name__) rather than configuring the root logger directly?

options.label: __name__ creates a hierarchical logger named after the module, allowing callers to selectively filter or configure logs per module
The root logger cannot write to console
Module loggers run in separate processes
__name__ is required by the Python garbage collector

questions.explanation: Using __name__ builds a dot-separated logger hierarchy reflecting package structure, giving application operators granular control over log levels per component.

questions.prompt: What happens in a finally block if the preceding try block executed a return statement?

options.label: The finally block is skipped completely
Python raises a ReturnCollisionError
The return statement is cancelled
The finally block executes before the function actually returns

questions.explanation: The finally block is guaranteed to execute before the function exits, even when a return statement was executed within the try or except blocks.

Files starting with test_ or ending with _test.py
Any Python file located inside a tests/ folder regardless of filename

try: parse_task("bad_input") except ValueError: pass

pytest.assert_raises(ValueError, parse_task, "bad_input")

tmp_path executes the test in an isolated Linux Docker container

Create one mutable dictionary as a module global and let every test edit it
Put the example dictionary in README.md and copy it manually before each run
Call pytest.main() inside every test to recreate the test process

questions.prompt: What happens when a test function in pytest finishes executing without encountering an AssertionError or unhandled exception?

options.label: pytest reports the test as skipped
pytest prompts the user for manual confirmation
pytest considers the test PASSED
pytest runs the test a second time to ensure stability

questions.prompt: Why should unit tests avoid reading live environment variables directly from os.environ without mocking or isolation?

options.label: os.environ cannot be accessed inside test functions
External environment variables can cause test outcomes to vary unpredictably between different machines or developer setups
Reading os.environ causes pytest to abort test execution immediately
Environment variables in Python are deleted after every test run

questions.explanation: Relying on external ambient state violates determinism; tests may pass locally on one machine but fail in CI or on another developer's workstation.

questions.prompt: Where should shared pytest fixtures used across multiple test files in a directory be placed?

options.label: In an __init__.py file in the project root
In a conftest.py file within the tests directory
In a global requirements.txt file
In the system site-packages folder

questions.prompt: What is the effect of passing the -v flag when running pytest in the terminal?

It validates the Python grammar without running tests
It enables verbose output, displaying each individual test name and its pass/fail result
It prints the version of pytest and immediately exits

questions.prompt: HTTPX applies a five-second network-inactivity timeout by default. Why should ApiClient still configure and document an explicit timeout?

options.label: An explicit timeout is required before response.json() can decode data
It makes the application’s latency budget intentional, reviewable, and independently adjustable for connect, read, write, or pool waits
It disables every HTTP error response below status 500
It guarantees that every request finishes successfully within that time

questions.explanation: HTTPX does not wait indefinitely by default: it raises after five seconds of network inactivity unless configured otherwise. An explicit application value still documents and enforces the product’s chosen latency policy; it does not guarantee success.

questions.prompt: An API call returns an HTTP 404 status code. What category of HTTP error does this represent?

options.label: A successful informational response
A transient server internal fault suitable for immediate retry
A client error indicating the requested resource does not exist on the server
A network gateway routing timeout

questions.explanation: HTTP 4xx status codes signify client-side errors (such as missing resources or invalid parameters), which should not be blindly retried without changing the request.

questions.prompt: How does httpx.MockTransport allow testing an HTTP client without making real internet connections?

options.label: By intercepting outgoing requests and executing custom mock response handler functions in memory
By disabling the computer network adapter during test runs
By writing requests to a local temporary text file
By converting HTTP calls into DNS queries

questions.explanation: httpx.MockTransport replaces the low-level transport layer with an in-memory handler, returning pre-programmed httpx.Response instances instantly without network I/O.

questions.prompt: Under what condition is it safe and recommended to automatically retry a failed HTTP request?

options.label: When the server returns 401 Unauthorized
When the server returns 422 Unprocessable Entity
When the request is an idempotent operation (e.g. GET) and failed due to a transient 503 or connection timeout
Whenever any error occurs, up to 100 consecutive attempts

questions.explanation: Retrying is appropriate for idempotent requests facing transient issues (e.g. 503 Service Unavailable, connection resets); non-idempotent or client-error requests should not be blindly repeated.

questions.prompt: What does response.raise_for_status() do when an HTTPX response has a status outside the successful 2xx range?

options.label: It rewrites the response as status 200 and returns it
It raises httpx.HTTPStatusError with request and response context
It retries the request with exponential backoff automatically
It raises httpx.TimeoutException regardless of the status

questions.explanation: HTTPX raise_for_status() raises HTTPStatusError for non-2xx response categories, including redirects as well as client and server errors. Retry policy remains the application’s responsibility.

questions.prompt: Why is exponential backoff with jitter preferred over a fixed retry delay when contacting external APIs?

options.label: It compresses HTTP request payload bodies
It prevents the thundering herd problem where all failing clients retry simultaneously and overwhelm the recovering server
It forces the operating system to allocate more memory to the client
It bypasses API rate limits permanently

questions.explanation: Exponential backoff increases wait times progressively, while jitter randomizes intervals to prevent synchronized bursts of retry traffic from crashing recovering services.

questions.prompt: What is the correct way to parse a JSON response payload using httpx?

options.label: json.loads(response.headers["content-type"])
response.to_json()
response.json()
str(response.content)

questions.explanation: The response.json() method decodes the response body bytes into Python native dictionaries or lists using the standard json parser.

questions.prompt: Inside an httpx.MockTransport handler, which behavior most directly simulates a client-side read timeout for an offline unit test?

options.label: Raise httpx.ReadTimeout("timed out", request=request)
Return httpx.Response(408, request=request)
Return httpx.Response(503, json={"error": "slow"}, request=request)
Return httpx.Response(200, content=b"")

questions.explanation: Raising ReadTimeout exercises the client’s timeout-exception path without a network. A 408, 503, or empty 200 is a completed HTTP response and therefore tests status/content handling instead.

questions.prompt: Which HTTP verb is defined by RFC specifications as inherently idempotent?

options.label: POST
PATCH
GET
CONNECT

questions.explanation: GET, PUT, and DELETE are defined as idempotent: performing multiple identical requests should produce the same state outcome on the server as a single request.

questions.prompt: If an API client catches httpx.TimeoutException, what domain-level action is most appropriate before deciding to retry?

options.label: Terminate the entire operating system process
Log the user password and send the request again immediately
Delete the virtual environment
Check if the request was idempotent and within retry budget before sleeping with backoff

questions.explanation: Timeout handling must verify that the operation is safe to repeat, check remaining retry attempts, and apply backoff rather than retrying blindly or crashing.

Either(int, None)
int or None
Nullable[int]

questions.prompt: Which Git command creates a new local Git repository in the current directory?

git setup
git init

questions.prompt: By default, what relationship do Python type annotations have to runtime argument enforcement?

options.label: Python compiles every annotated function to machine code before it can run
Python stores annotation metadata but does not automatically reject mismatched argument values; a checker such as mypy analyzes the declared contract separately
Every annotation automatically invokes Pydantic validation at runtime
Annotated functions can run only while a type checker process is active

questions.prompt: What does adding .venv/ to .gitignore do in a repository?

options.label: It tells Git to normally ignore that currently untracked path; a file already tracked in the index needs a separate removal-from-index step
It deletes .venv from disk and from every previous commit
It encrypts the directory before Git sends it to a remote
It prevents Python from activating the virtual environment

questions.prompt: How do you configure argparse to require a subcommand (such as "run" or "status") rather than allowing the program to execute without one?

parser.enable_subcommands(mandatory=True)
parser.set_subcommand_flag()
subparsers.is_required = 1

questions.prompt: What contract is communicated by def run_check(name: str, retries: int) -> bool?

options.label: The function accepts any number of unnamed arguments and returns a string
Python will automatically convert every supplied value to the annotated type
Callers should supply a string and an integer, and the function returns a Boolean; a static checker can flag incompatible calls
The function can be called only from a dataclass method

questions.explanation: The annotations describe parameter and return types for readers and static tools. They do not by themselves convert values or guarantee runtime rejection.

questions.prompt: A developer stages changes using git add . and then runs git commit -m "Add doctor subcommand". Where are these changes recorded?

options.label: Directly on the remote GitHub server
In the local Git repository history
In the Python virtual environment
In the Windows Registry

questions.prompt: What argparse argument type converts a command-line parameter like "--port 8080" directly into a Python integer?

parser.add_argument("--port", convert=int)

cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = %s" % user_input)

It automatically commits transactions on success, or rolls back if an unhandled exception occurs
It converts all tables to temporary in-memory tables
It closes the connection immediately

questions.prompt: What happens when a coroutine directly calls blocking code such as time.sleep() or requests.get()?

asyncio.TaskGroup

Call each coroutine without awaiting it
Run asyncio.run() separately for each coroutine inside the event loop

The process exits immediately
The context cancels the work and raises TimeoutError outside the context

Returning a refusal to a prohibited request
Recording a redacted audit event

Increase model response latency
Make a public tool return fewer fields

A mistaken or injected action can materially alter the host system

skillCheck.instructions: Answer all 10 questions. A score of 7/10 (70%) passes. Review the explanations before any recovery attempt.

questions.prompt: What does the Dependency Inversion Principle require of high-level agent orchestration code?

options.label: Every module must instantiate its own dependencies
High-level and low-level code should depend on abstractions
Concrete infrastructure should import the application entry point
Dependency injection requires a third-party container framework

questions.explanation: High-level policy should depend on stable abstractions rather than concrete database, model, or tool implementations.

questions.prompt: What can happen when module A and module B import each other at module-import time?

options.label: One module may be only partially initialized, causing import-time failures
Python always resolves the cycle without observable effects
The interpreter always raises SyntaxError
Both modules are automatically merged

questions.explanation: A cycle may expose a partially initialized module and raise an ImportError or AttributeError depending on access order; it does not have one guaranteed error.

questions.prompt: Why give specialist agents bounded tool subsets instead of exposing every tool to every specialist?

options.label: It guarantees every specialist reaches the same answer
It removes the need for permission enforcement
It improves relevance and reduces unnecessary capability exposure
It allows specialists to bypass the orchestrator

questions.explanation: A smaller relevant capability surface improves selection clarity and limits the impact of errors or compromised context.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a true agent handoff from a manager calling a specialist as a tool?

options.label: A handoff merely changes the Python function name
A handoff means two agents always run concurrently
A handoff keeps all control with the manager
A handoff transfers active control/responsibility to the specialist

questions.explanation: A handoff transfers active control and conversation responsibility; a manager-as-tool pattern keeps control with the manager and receives a bounded result.

questions.prompt: What is the job of an application composition root?

options.label: Construct and wire concrete dependencies at one application boundary
Store every domain rule in global variables
Generate model answers before startup
Make each package import all other packages

questions.explanation: The composition root is the boundary that constructs concrete dependencies and connects them to high-level abstractions.

questions.prompt: What special module variable controls names imported by `from package import *`?

options.label: __name__
__path__
__all__
__exports__

questions.explanation: __all__ explicitly lists the public names used by wildcard import; explicit imports may still access other module attributes.

questions.prompt: How does typing.Protocol make a high-level orchestrator easier to test?

options.label: It executes every test in a separate process
Fakes can satisfy the required interface structurally
It automatically mocks every method call
It prevents runtime exceptions

questions.explanation: A fake only needs to satisfy the required structural interface, so tests can replace network or persistence implementations without inheritance coupling.

questions.prompt: What context should a manager provide to a specialist for a bounded delegated task?

options.label: Every secret and all application state
Only the specialist name
The complete raw history regardless of relevance
The bounded objective, relevant context, constraints, capabilities, and output contract

questions.explanation: Pass the objective, relevant evidence and constraints, allowed capabilities, and expected result shape—not unrelated secrets or the entire history by default.

questions.prompt: Where should a modular application normally assemble concrete gateways, repositories, registries, and policies?

options.label: In a composition root at the application boundary
Inside every domain entity
Inside package __init__ wildcard imports
In the model prompt

questions.explanation: A composition root centralizes construction and wiring without leaking concrete dependencies into domain logic.

questions.prompt: Why separate deterministic planning rules from network, database, and model I/O behind narrow interfaces?

options.label: To ensure domain code never accepts input
To make every operation synchronous
To test policy deterministically and replace infrastructure without rewriting it
To eliminate the need for integration tests

questions.explanation: The deterministic core can be tested quickly with fakes, while infrastructure changes or failures remain localized.

steps.text: Create pyproject.toml with an explicit standards-based build backend, PEP 621 metadata, requires-python, runtime dependencies, package discovery, and named development/test dependency configuration supported by the chosen tooling.
Define [project.scripts] pyae = "pyae.cli:main" and make the CLI return useful --help and --version output without importing optional provider clients or requiring secrets.

Configuration follows the deploy-varying environment boundary, validates values, and fails early without exposing or inventing required secrets.
CI syntax is valid and each supported Python matrix job runs the documented lint, type, test, build, and fresh-wheel smoke commands.
All required CI tests and smoke commands use FakeModel or local fixtures and require no live provider token or external service.

hints: Editable install proves the development loop; only a fresh installation of the built wheel exposes missing files and undeclared dependencies.
Use python -m build as the portable artifact build; add backend-specific checks only as supplemental validation.
Keep required secrets conditional on the selected provider so --help and the offline mode remain usable.

questions.prompt: Under PEP 621, where is standard project metadata such as name, version, and dependencies declared?

setup.py only
The [project] table in pyproject.toml
The package __init__.py file

questions.prompt: What does `python -m pip install -e .` do for a local project?

options.label: Installs an editable development link to the local source
Builds and uploads a release to PyPI
Installs only test dependencies
Copies the source into a Docker image

questions.explanation: It installs the project in editable mode so source changes are normally reflected without rebuilding/reinstalling, while dependencies and entry points are installed.

questions.prompt: Which pyproject.toml entry defines a `pyae` command that calls `main` in `pyae.cli`?

options.label: [tool.cli] pyae = "pyae.cli.main"
[project.scripts] pyae = "pyae.cli:main"
[build-system] pyae = "pyae/cli.py"
[project.urls] pyae = "pyae.cli:main"

questions.explanation: The [project.scripts] table maps a command name to an importable object reference.

questions.prompt: What configuration rule is described by the Twelve-Factor App?

options.label: Keep all environment values in package source
Use the same credential in every deployment
Treat internal constants as deploy-time secrets
Store deploy-varying configuration in environment variables

questions.explanation: Deploy-varying configuration, especially credentials and service endpoints, belongs in the environment rather than committed source.

questions.prompt: In GitHub Actions, which top-level key defines events such as push that trigger a workflow?

options.label: on
runs-on
jobs
uses

questions.explanation: The top-level on key declares workflow trigger events.

questions.prompt: Why separate runtime dependencies from development or test dependencies in project metadata?

options.label: It prevents runtime packages from receiving security updates
It makes dependency versions unnecessary
It avoids shipping test tooling to normal users while keeping development setup reproducible
It guarantees optional packages are imported lazily

questions.explanation: Separation keeps normal installs minimal while named development groups or extras install tooling only where needed; the exact mechanism depends on project and backend support.

questions.prompt: Which command performs the essential standards-based check that a source tree can produce distribution artifacts?

options.label: python -m pip freeze
python -m build
python -m http.server
python -m pytest --collect-only

questions.explanation: `python -m build` invokes the configured build backend in isolation and should produce the source distribution and wheel; other validators can add checks but do not replace the build.

questions.prompt: Why install the built wheel in a fresh virtual environment before release?

options.label: It verifies that the artifact installs and runs without relying on the source checkout
It proves every future operating system is supported
It replaces all unit and integration tests
It automatically publishes the wheel

questions.explanation: A clean install catches missing package data, undeclared dependencies, and entry-point mistakes that an editable source checkout can hide.

questions.prompt: How should startup behave when a credential required for the selected provider is absent?

options.label: Generate a placeholder credential and continue
Log every environment variable for diagnosis
Wait until the first remote call fails ambiguously
Fail early with a clear validation error that does not expose secrets

questions.explanation: Required configuration should fail early with a clear, non-secret error rather than inventing a default or failing deep inside a request.

questions.prompt: Why run CI against each Python version the project claims to support?

options.label: It makes all versions execute identical machine code
It detects compatibility failures across the declared support range
It removes the need to specify requires-python
It guarantees third-party services remain available

questions.explanation: The matrix reveals interpreter and dependency differences before users encounter them and makes the support claim executable.

skillCheck.instructions: Answer all 10 questions. A score of 7/10 (70%) passes. Review the explanations before any recovery attempt.

questions.prompt: Which property most clearly distinguishes an agent loop from a one-shot script that calls a model once?

options.label: It iteratively selects actions from observations until a stopping condition
It always uses more than one model provider
It must run continuously in the cloud
It never asks a human for confirmation

questions.explanation: An agent loop observes state, selects actions/tools, incorporates results, and iterates toward a stopping condition.

questions.prompt: Which personal-agent actions should require an explicit human confirmation gate?

options.label: Every action including formatting local text
Only actions whose tool name contains delete
Actions classified as high impact, destructive, costly, sensitive, or externally side-effecting
No action once the system prompt calls the user trusted

questions.explanation: Policy should classify actions by impact and reversibility; destructive, external side-effecting, costly, or sensitive actions need confirmation, while harmless reads need not all be blocked.

questions.prompt: How can a team gain fast confidence in ordinary agent code changes without paid model calls?

options.label: Skip model-boundary tests entirely
Use deterministic fakes, fixtures, integration tests, and offline regression evals
Retry live calls until outputs match
Replace assertions with manual screenshots

questions.explanation: Deterministic fake gateways, tool fixtures, integration scenarios, and offline evals test contracts repeatedly; periodic live checks remain a separate layer.

questions.prompt: What operational value does structured step-level JSONL tracing provide?

options.label: A queryable record of observable steps, timing, calls, results, and failures
A guaranteed record of every private model thought
Automatic authorization for traced actions
A replacement for secret redaction

questions.explanation: It records observable decisions, calls, timing, results, and errors for diagnosis without claiming access to private internal model reasoning.

questions.prompt: When is SQLite with write-ahead logging a reasonable persistence choice for a personal agent?

options.label: For every distributed multi-region workload
Whenever multiple hosts must write one network-mounted file
Only when durability is unnecessary
For suitable local transactional workloads after checking concurrency and filesystem constraints

questions.explanation: It fits many local, single-machine workloads needing transactions and useful read concurrency, but suitability depends on filesystem, write contention, and deployment needs.

questions.prompt: Why rerun regression benchmarks after changing a system prompt or tool description?

options.label: To guarantee the prompt is subjectively better
To detect behavior, safety, and efficiency regressions against stable cases
To eliminate the need for code tests
To make every model response deterministic

questions.explanation: Those changes can alter selection and behavior; stable cases reveal lost capabilities, safety regressions, and cost shifts.

questions.prompt: Why validate tool arguments against a strict schema before application logic runs?

options.label: To authorize every schema-valid action automatically
To hide tool descriptions from the model
To reject malformed input before execution while authorization remains separate
To convert all tools into read-only operations

questions.explanation: Early validation rejects missing, malformed, or out-of-range input before it reaches a side-effect boundary.

questions.prompt: Which strategy best addresses indirect prompt injection from retrieved documents?

options.label: Layer untrusted-data framing with least privilege, validation, authorization, and confirmation
Trust retrieved instructions after adding XML tags
Use a single regex to delete the word ignore
Give the retrieval model every tool so it can verify content

questions.explanation: Defense in depth combines untrusted-data separation with least privilege, deterministic authorization, validation, confirmation, and safe output handling; no single prompt technique is sufficient.

questions.prompt: What practical benefit comes from packaging the agent with standard metadata and a CLI entry point?

options.label: It makes the application secure without policy checks
It guarantees compatibility with every Python version
It removes the need for documentation
It provides a reproducible installation and stable way to run the application

questions.explanation: A standard install and stable command make setup, dependency resolution, execution, testing, and distribution reproducible.

questions.prompt: What long-term benefit does a provider-neutral gateway abstraction offer?

options.label: Every provider becomes behaviorally identical
Provider outages can no longer affect the agent
Provider-specific change is localized behind a stable application contract
No adapter tests are needed

questions.explanation: It localizes provider-specific change and makes substitution/testing easier; it cannot promise seamless switching when capabilities differ.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A project-local Python installation area with its own packages.
concepts.example: Create `.venv`, activate it, then install packages through `python -m pip`.
concepts.commonMistake: Treating `.venv` as project source or committing its machine-specific files.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A program controlled through terminal commands, arguments, and text output.
concepts.example: `python doctor.py` runs a diagnostic and prints labeled results.
concepts.commonMistake: Mixing input/output code into every business function.

concepts.simpleMeaning: Data that exists only while the current process is running.
concepts.example: A dictionary stores tasks until the CLI exits.
concepts.commonMistake: Assuming an in-memory dictionary survives an application restart.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A function whose result depends on its inputs and which does not secretly change outside state.
concepts.example: `priority_score(task)` returns a number without printing or editing a file.
concepts.commonMistake: Calling a function pure while it reads globals, performs I/O, or mutates its arguments.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A named structure that describes the fields and meaning of one kind of record.
concepts.example: A `Task` dataclass defines `id`, `title`, `priority`, and `completed`.
concepts.commonMistake: Using unrelated dictionary keys everywhere without one agreed record shape.

concepts.simpleMeaning: Giving each module one clear responsibility and a small interface to the others.
concepts.example: `models.py` describes tasks, `service.py` transforms them, and `cli.py` handles the terminal.
concepts.commonMistake: Splitting files while leaving circular imports or duplicated responsibilities.

concepts.simpleMeaning: Replacing a complete file in one operation so a crash cannot expose a half-written target.
concepts.example: Write valid JSON to a sibling temporary file, then call `temp_path.replace(state_path)`.
concepts.commonMistake: Writing directly over the only good state file.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A stored number that identifies the shape of persisted data.
concepts.example: `{"schema_version": 1, "tasks": []}` lets future code detect older formats.
concepts.commonMistake: Changing stored structure without a version or migration path.

concepts.simpleMeaning: Raising a domain-specific error while preserving the original failure as its cause.
concepts.example: `raise StorageCorruptionError() from error` keeps the JSON traceback.
concepts.commonMistake: Replacing the original exception with a vague message and losing diagnostic evidence.

concepts.simpleMeaning: Recording consistent named fields so events can be searched and compared.
concepts.example: Each record includes timestamp, level, operation, and task ID.
concepts.commonMistake: Logging secrets or building unsearchable free-form messages for every event.

concepts.simpleMeaning: Reusable setup that gives a test controlled starting data or resources.
concepts.example: A pytest fixture returns a fresh task collection for each test.
concepts.commonMistake: Sharing mutable fixture state so one test changes another test’s result.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A controlled replacement for a real dependency during a test.
concepts.example: MockTransport returns an HTTP 503 without contacting the internet.
concepts.commonMistake: Calling a live service and calling the result a deterministic unit test.

concepts.simpleMeaning: Repeating the same operation has the same intended effect as doing it once.
concepts.example: Retrying a GET should not create another record.
concepts.commonMistake: Retrying a state-changing request without knowing whether the first attempt succeeded.

concepts.simpleMeaning: Waiting progressively longer between bounded retries.
concepts.example: Retry after roughly 1, 2, then 4 seconds and stop at the retry limit.
concepts.commonMistake: Retrying forever or having every client retry at the same instant.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A tool checks declared value shapes before execution while Python remains dynamically executed.
concepts.example: A checker flags passing `str` to a function declared to accept `int`.
concepts.commonMistake: Assuming annotations automatically validate values at runtime.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A named action beneath one terminal program, with its own arguments and help.
concepts.example: `pyae doctor` and `pyae tasks` share one parser but dispatch different work.
concepts.commonMistake: Building one large parser branch with unclear help and no required command.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A typed description of required methods that compatible classes can satisfy without inheritance.
concepts.example: Any class with the declared `generate` signature can satisfy `ModelGateway` during static checking.
concepts.commonMistake: Assuming a Protocol automatically performs complete runtime validation.

concepts.simpleMeaning: One application-owned boundary through which the rest of the system requests model output.
concepts.example: The extractor calls `gateway.generate(messages)` rather than a vendor SDK.
concepts.commonMistake: Scattering provider-specific calls and response shapes across the application.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A deterministic model replacement that returns scripted responses and records requests.
concepts.example: A test supplies malformed JSON followed by valid JSON without network access.
concepts.commonMistake: Calling a paid live model in a test that must be repeatable.

concepts.simpleMeaning: Model output constrained to a known machine-readable shape.
concepts.example: A task extraction must validate as a Pydantic model.
concepts.commonMistake: Trusting text that merely looks like JSON without parsing and validation.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A limited retry that returns concrete validation errors so output can be corrected.
concepts.example: On invalid JSON, return the exact error and allow at most two repair attempts.
concepts.commonMistake: Retrying indefinitely or hiding why validation failed.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A document that describes allowed JSON types, properties, and required fields.
concepts.example: A tool schema requires a string `path` property.
concepts.commonMistake: Treating a prose tool description as parameter validation.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A boundary that selects a registered handler and invokes it only after validating the request.
concepts.example: The dispatcher maps `read_file` to its callable after checking arguments.
concepts.commonMistake: Executing an arbitrary name supplied by a model.

concepts.simpleMeaning: The limited amount of input and output a model can consider in one request.
concepts.example: Older turns are pruned when the estimated message total exceeds the budget.
concepts.commonMistake: Assuming conversation history can grow forever.

concepts.simpleMeaning: Replacing older detail with a smaller summary while preserving required facts.
concepts.example: Keep the system message and latest turn, then summarize older completed work.
concepts.commonMistake: Dropping tool-call pairs or safety instructions independently.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A bounded cycle that asks a model, executes an allowed action, records the observation, and decides whether to continue.
concepts.example: Predict → validate action → act → observe → stop or repeat.
concepts.commonMistake: Using an unbounded `while True` loop with no explicit terminal states.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A rule that detects repeated equivalent actions and stops an unproductive loop.
concepts.example: Abort after the same tool and arguments appear three consecutive times.
concepts.commonMistake: Counting only step number while allowing identical harmful actions to repeat.

concepts.simpleMeaning: Granting only the capabilities required for the current task.
concepts.example: A reading task receives a workspace read tool but no shell or delete tool.
concepts.commonMistake: Giving every agent every available tool for convenience.

concepts.simpleMeaning: Resolving a requested path and proving it remains inside an allowed root before access.
concepts.example: Reject a resolved `..\secret.txt` target outside the workspace.
concepts.commonMistake: Checking the raw path string before resolving parents and links.

concepts.simpleMeaning: An ordered, versioned change that moves stored data from one schema to the next.
concepts.example: `PRAGMA user_version` selects which migration runs next.
concepts.commonMistake: Editing an old migration after users may already have applied it.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A small interface that owns persistence operations for application data.
concepts.example: `save_message` and `get_recent_messages` hide SQL from the agent loop.
concepts.commonMistake: Letting UI, model, and policy code each issue unrelated SQL.

concepts.simpleMeaning: Answering from selected source passages and preserving where each claim came from.
concepts.example: Return a passage with file path and line range, then require citations.
concepts.commonMistake: Adding retrieved text without provenance or an answer-when-missing rule.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A lexical relevance score that balances matching terms against document length and term rarity.
concepts.example: FTS5 orders matching chunks with `bm25(documents_fts)`.
concepts.commonMistake: Treating the score as proof that a passage answers the question.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A versioned set of representative inputs and expected behaviors.
concepts.example: Each case records the prompt, expected tool calls, and acceptable answer evidence.
concepts.commonMistake: Testing only one happy-path example chosen after seeing the output.

concepts.simpleMeaning: Checking the actions and observations used to reach a result, not only the final wording.
concepts.example: Verify that search occurred before a grounded answer.
concepts.commonMistake: Scoring hidden chain-of-thought instead of observable actions and outcomes.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A timed record for one operation inside a larger traced run.
concepts.example: A tool-call span stores trace ID, span ID, parent ID, start time, and duration.
concepts.commonMistake: Using logs and traces as synonyms without preserving causal relationships.

concepts.simpleMeaning: An explicit mapping from a failure category to retry, report, preserve-state, or stop behavior.
concepts.example: Retry a transient rate limit within budget; stop and preserve state on a fatal error.
concepts.commonMistake: Catching every exception and pretending execution succeeded.

concepts.simpleMeaning: Concurrent tasks are started and completed within a scope that owns their cancellation and errors.
concepts.example: A TaskGroup cancels sibling tasks when one fails and waits for cleanup.
concepts.commonMistake: Starting background tasks with no owner or shutdown path.

concepts.simpleMeaning: Untrusted content contains instructions intended to override the agent’s real task or policy.
concepts.example: A retrieved file says to reveal secrets instead of answering the user’s question.
concepts.commonMistake: Treating keyword detection as a complete security boundary.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A deterministic table mapping actions and roles to allowed, denied, or confirmation-required decisions.
concepts.example: Reading may be automatic while writing requires approval.
concepts.commonMistake: Relying on a system prompt to enforce permissions.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A protocol through which a host discovers and invokes capabilities exposed by an external server.
concepts.example: A client initializes a stdio session, lists tools, and calls one validated tool.
concepts.commonMistake: Trusting a discovered server or tool definition without review.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A request/response message format with method names, parameters, IDs, results, and errors.
concepts.example: A `tools/list` request includes `jsonrpc`, `id`, and `method`.
concepts.commonMistake: Confusing the message format with the transport carrying it.

concepts.simpleMeaning: High-level behavior depends on an application-owned abstraction rather than a concrete external service.
concepts.example: AgentRunner receives a ModelGateway Protocol implementation.
concepts.commonMistake: Moving constructors to one file while domain modules still import concrete infrastructure.

concepts.simpleMeaning: The one startup location that creates concrete services and wires them together.
concepts.example: `AgentContainer` constructs the gateway, repository, tools, and policies.
concepts.commonMistake: Using a container as a global service locator throughout the codebase.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A coordinator gives a bounded subtask and necessary context to a specialist, then receives a result.
concepts.example: The research specialist receives only the query and approved read tools.
concepts.commonMistake: Passing the entire conversation and every tool without a clear contract.

concepts.simpleMeaning: Metadata that maps an installed terminal command to a Python callable.
concepts.example: `pyae = "pyae.cli:main"` creates the `pyae` command after installation.
concepts.commonMistake: Depending on the repository working directory or manual `sys.path` edits.

concepts.simpleMeaning: Automated checks that run from a clean environment whenever relevant code changes.
concepts.example: A GitHub Actions job installs the package and runs tests on Python 3.12.
concepts.commonMistake: Adding tools to CI that the project never declares or can reproduce locally.

concepts.simpleMeaning: Connecting previously verified components into one system and checking their boundaries together.
concepts.example: The packaged CLI uses the gateway, tools, memory, retrieval, security, tracing, and evals.
concepts.commonMistake: Adding new major features during the final integration week.
